I've been farming these fields in Quzhou for over fifty years, and at seventy, my back hurts and my knees aren't what they used to be, but I still know this land better than anyone. My family has only two and a half mu — my son works in the city and sends money home, but I won't let good land go to waste. 

This year, like every year, I'll plant winter wheat in the autumn on all my land. Wheat is my backbone — I need the flour for my own food, and the leftover grain brings in cash. I'll use the improved Jinmai seed I've been saving and swapping with neighbors; it grows well here and I'm used to its temperament. Before planting, I'll run the rotary tiller over the field to break up the soil. I'll put down about 20 jin of nitrogen fertilizer per mu, some phosphorus, and a bit of potassium — I don't measure like the young technicians from the university, but I know by hand and by bag how much the soil needs. I'll irrigate four times: at planting, before winter sets in, at jointing when the wheat shoots up, and once more when the grain is filling. I'll spray twice for weeds and bugs, because if I don't, the armyworms and aphids will steal my crop.

After I harvest the wheat in early June, I won't waste a single day — I'll plant summer maize right away. Everyone here grows maize after wheat; the land is hot and ready. I'll buy hybrid seed from the village supply store; I've learned that hybrid maize gives bigger ears, and even though the seed costs money, it's worth it. I won't till much — just plant directly into the wheat stubble to save time and strength. Maize needs water when it's silking, so I'll irrigate twice if the summer rains don't come. I'll fertilize once at planting and once when it's knee-high. Two sprays should keep the pests away.

I don't try fancy new crops anymore. At my age, I stick to what feeds me and what I can manage alone. Wheat and maize, twice a year, on my two and a half mu. That's my life, and it works.
